title: Speculative shared tokenization layer to cut prefill-side overhead for common prefixes
creator: Ethan Cole
description:
Problem: A measurable portion of end-to-end request latency (prefill side) is dominated by prompt preprocessing: tokenizer latency, repeated encoding of identical or highly-similar prefixes (system messages, instructions, few-shot demonstration blocks), and expensive context-copy/serialize costs before KV prefill begins. This is especially visible for low-token decode workloads where prefill overhead is a large fraction of total latency.

Goal: Implement a speculative shared tokenization layer and inflight deduplication to: (1) eliminate redundant tokenization for identical prefixes across concurrent requests; (2) publish tokenized prefixes earlier so the serving runtime can start KV prefill and kernel selection sooner; (3) provide a fast-path for short/known prefixes that matches the hot path used in high-throughput flows. Target: reduce median prefill-side latency by 30% and 95th by 20% for workloads with repeated prefixes, and reduce CPU tokenization cycles by ~40% on benchmark traces.

Design overview:
- Prefix fingerprinting: compute stable fingerprint for prefix text using incremental 64-bit hash keyed by customer and route (to avoid cross-tenant leakage).
- Shared prefix cache: LRU segmented cache in front of runtime (hot-path) that stores: raw prefix length, token ids array, attention mask template, and metadata (model-compatibility tags, tokenization-version). TTLs are conservative (default 5m) and eviction respects per-customer memory quotas.
- Inflight dedup: when first request for a fingerprint arrives, mark entry as IN_FLIGHT and run tokenization once; subsequent requests wait on a lightweight future or subscribe to the tokenized result. Use a bounded wait window to avoid head-of-line blocking for slow or large prefixes.
- Early publish / speculative prefill: once token ids for the prefix are available, emit a prefill intent event to the runtime control plane to start KV warming and kernel selection. This lets the serving runtime begin memory allocation and schedule kernels while the rest of request is being prepared.
- CPU tokenization workers: separate pool of pinned tokenization workers with affinity to NUMA nodes; avoid user request threads doing expensive tokenization. Provide batching of tokenization tasks up to 32 prefixes.
- Compatibility: cache entries include model-compatibility and tokenizer-version; if model mismatch, fallback to per-request tokenization. Provide opt-out via header for customers with highly-sensitive prompts.

Trade-offs and constraints:
- Memory: caching token arrays increases RAM usage; mitigated by segmented per-tenant quotas and compact token storage (uint16/uint32 depending on vocab size).
- Freshness: short TTL may reduce hit rate; long TTL increases staleness if tokenizer changes. We will attach tokenizer-version to cache key and invalidate on model/tokenizer updates.
- Security: must ensure no cross-tenant leakage through sharing; all cache keys include tenant id and route. Security review required before rollout to private deployments.
- Complexity: inflight dedup introduces blocking points; we cap wait times and provide fallback paths.

Non-goals: full semantic deduplication of paraphrases, or automatic normalization of prompt content. This ticket is focused on exact-prefix and near-identical-string reuse for production common prefixes (system prompts, templates, starter kits).
acceptance_criteria: Cache stores tokenized prefixes and serves hits for identical tenant+route+tokenizer-version fingerprints
In-flight dedup prevents duplicate tokenization for concurrent requests with same fingerprint without increasing 95th percentile tail above baseline
End-to-end benchmarks on curated production traces show >=30% median reduction in prefill-side latency for repeated-prefix traffic and total CPU tokenization cycles reduced by >=30%
Feature has config toggle and per-tenant memory quota; secure by design (no cross-tenant leakage) and passes security review checklist
Observability added: hit/miss/inflight metrics, cache memory usage, top fingerprint histogram, and dashboard link in Console
comments: 2026-03-01 - Ethan Cole: Initial RFC attached; spike results show 27-42% CPU savings on two sample apps when prefix reuse >20% (conservative traces). See Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Speculative+Prefix+Tokenization

2026-03-03 - Sofia Patel: Prototype of shared cache implemented in the prefill service. Inflight dedup implemented with a small future-based waitlist. Created draft PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1258

2026-03-04 - Miguel Hernandez (review): Nice approach, request that we add tokenizer-version to cache key and ensure invalidation hook ties into model deploy pipeline. Also want gauge for waiting subscribers to detect blocking storms. Added as follow-up task.

2026-03-05 - QA: Load test with 2k rps synthetic workload that includes common prefix showed median prefill latency improvement from 62ms -> 38ms and 95th from 210ms -> 176ms. Memory pressure observed on a single node; will add per-tenant quota enforcement. See Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/abcd123/prefix-cache-overview

2026-03-06 - Design (Ava Chen): Reviewed UX for Console exposure of cache-explainability; suggested per-route breakdown and top fingerprints UI. Filed design ticket DES-1642 for console filter and tooltip copy.

2026-03-08 - Security (Priya Rao): Raised concern about log leakage while populating cache and requested that token arrays are stored in encrypted process memory and never serialized to logs. Security review checklist assigned. Blocker until encryption-in-memory primitive is validated.

2026-03-10 - Sofia Patel: Implemented tenant-scoped quotas and tokenizer-version keying. Added metric for wait queue length and fallback timer. Updated PR with unit tests and integration tests. Next: run extended soak and schedule security review meeting.
